segments.text: Secant lines approach a tangent line
Secant lines through P = (1, 48) approach the tangent line as the second point moves toward P.

visuals.learningPurpose: Connect average velocity over a nonzero time interval to instantaneous velocity as the second point approaches P.
visuals.longDescription: A position curve s(t) = 64t - 16t squared is shown from 0 to 4 seconds. P is fixed at t = 1 second and s = 48 feet. Three secant states through P have slopes 16, 24, and 28.8 feet per second. The active secant can use positive or negative nonzero h and rotates toward the tangent line, whose slope is 32 feet per second.

presentation.colorIndependentCue: Heavy solid position curve.
Dotted reference secant for h = 1.
Dashed reference secant for h = 0.5.
Heavy active secant controlled by the nonzero h step control.
Double-stroked tangent line through P.
Filled circle labeled P at (1, 48).
Filled diamond labeled Q distinguishes the movable point from P.
Text annotation states both slope formulas.

controls.announcementTemplate: h is {value}; the secant slope is 32 minus 16h feet per second.

accessibility.ariaLabel: Interactive graph of secant lines approaching the tangent to a position curve.
accessibility.summary: P stays fixed while nonzero h moves Q and changes the secant slope toward 32 feet per second.
accessibility.colorIndependentDescription: The position curve is heavy and solid, reference secants are dotted and dashed, the active secant is heavy, and the tangent is double-stroked. P is a circle and Q is a diamond.
accessibility.keyboardInstructions: Focus the h control and use its step commands. Zero is intentionally absent because a secant requires two distinct points.
controlInstructions: Choose positive or negative nonzero h values and compare the announced secant slope with 32.

A limit at a removable hole
The function is undefined at x = 2, but nearby outputs approach 4.

visuals.learningPurpose: Show that a two-sided limit depends on nearby outputs even when the function is undefined at the target input.
visuals.longDescription: The line y = x + 2 is drawn on two explicit domains, one to the left of 2 and one to the right. An open circle at (2, 4) marks the missing value. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides identify x = 2 and y = 4, so the common approached height remains clear without relying on color.

Unequal one-sided limits produce a jump and no two-sided limit.

visuals.learningPurpose: Show that a two-sided limit does not exist when finite left-hand and right-hand limits disagree.
visuals.longDescription: For x less than 2, the line y = x + 1 approaches the open circle (2, 3). For x at least 2, the line y = 6 - x begins at the filled diamond (2, 4). Text labels state that the left-hand limit is 3 and the right-hand limit is 4, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

The function sin(1/x) oscillates increasingly rapidly near zero and has no limit there.

visuals.learningPurpose: Demonstrate a limit failure caused by outputs oscillating indefinitely rather than approaching one value.
visuals.longDescription: Two explicit branches of y = sin(1/x) are drawn for negative and positive x near zero. The curve remains between -1 and 1 but swings more rapidly as x approaches zero. Neither domain includes zero, no segment connects across zero, and every neighborhood contains many high and low values instead of one approached height.

Solid oscillating branch starts after zero.

accessibility.ariaLabel: Two branches of sin(1/x) oscillating rapidly near zero.
accessibility.summary: The bounded outputs continue swinging between -1 and 1 in every neighborhood of zero, so no limit exists.
accessibility.colorIndependentDescription: Separate left and right solid branches leave a visible break at x = 0, and a text annotation names the infinite oscillation.

segments.text: The function sin(1/x) oscillates increasingly rapidly near zero and has no limit there.
An oscillating function squeezed to zero
The oscillating function is trapped between -x squared and x squared, both of which approach zero.

visuals.learningPurpose: Make the Squeeze Theorem visible by comparing an oscillating middle function with upper and lower bounds that share limit zero.
visuals.longDescription: The middle curve y = x squared times sin(1/x) oscillates on separate domains to the left and right of zero. A dashed upper curve y = x squared and a dotted lower curve y = negative x squared form a narrowing envelope. The middle curve remains inside that envelope, and all three approach zero. The middle formula is undefined at zero and is never connected across it.

For a unit circle and 0 < theta < pi/2, the inner triangle lies inside the sector, which lies inside the outer tangent triangle.

visuals.learningPurpose: Compare the areas of an inner triangle, circular sector, and outer tangent triangle to establish the inequalities behind the sine limit.
visuals.longDescription: A unit circle is centered at O = (0, 0). A = (1, 0), B = (cos theta, sin theta), and T = (1, tan theta). Segments form an inner triangle OAB and an outer tangent triangle OAT, while the circle arc and radii bound the sector AOB. Patterned regions and a written inequality show inner triangle area less than or equal to sector area less than or equal to outer triangle area.

Odd and even powers at a vertical asymptote
An odd power changes sign across the vertical asymptote; an even power remains positive on both sides.

visuals.longDescription: Two ordered panels share the vertical asymptote x = 1. In the odd-power panel, y = 1/(x - 1) falls without bound from the left and rises without bound from the right. In the even-power panel, y = 1/(x - 1) squared rises without bound from both sides. Each panel uses explicit left and right domains and a dashed asymptote.

The four principal discontinuity types encountered in first-semester calculus.

visuals.learningPurpose: Compare removable, jump, infinite, and oscillatory discontinuities in a consistent four-panel layout.
visuals.longDescription: A two-by-two gallery compares behavior at x = 0. Removable shows y = x + 1 with an open point at (0, 1). Jump shows y = 0 to the left and y = 2 to the right with open and filled markers. Infinite shows y = 1/x on split domains with a vertical asymptote. Oscillatory shows y = sin(1/x) on split domains that never settle near zero.

A root guaranteed by the Intermediate Value Theorem
Continuity and opposite endpoint signs guarantee at least one root between 0 and 1.

visuals.learningPurpose: Show how continuity and opposite endpoint signs guarantee at least one zero between the endpoints.
visuals.longDescription: The continuous curve f(x) = x cubed + x - 1 is shown on the closed interval from 0 to 1. A filled circle at (0, -1) lies below the x-axis and a filled square at (1, 1) lies above it. The curve crosses the axis at a filled diamond c approximately 0.6823, illustrating a root whose existence the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees.

An epsilon band and delta window
An epsilon band around L and a corresponding delta window around a. A valid delta keeps the nearby graph inside the band.

visuals.learningPurpose: Connect the output condition |f(x) - L| < epsilon to an input window 0 < |x - a| < delta on a nonlinear graph.
visuals.longDescription: The curve f(x) = x squared divided by 2 plus 1 passes through (a, L) = (2, 3). A horizontally patterned band extends from 3 - epsilon to 3 + epsilon. A vertically patterned window is bounded by 4 - square root of (4 + 2 epsilon) and square root of (4 + 2 epsilon). With epsilon 0.75, the largest symmetric delta is about 0.3452, and nearby curve points inside that punctured window remain in the output band.
